title: Minimum Spanning Tree
body:
Given a connected [[Weighted Graph]], a **spanning tree** is a subset of edges that touches
every vertex and contains no cycle. The **minimum** spanning tree is the one whose edge
weights add up to least. Connect every city, lay the least cable.

Counting says a spanning tree of $V$ vertices always has exactly $V - 1$ edges, whichever one
you pick: enough to connect everything, one short of a cycle. Adding any further edge closes
a cycle, removing any edge disconnects the graph. That is what makes it a [[Tree]].

```
    A --4-- B        edges: A-C 1, C-D 2, A-D 3, A-B 4, B-D 5
    |  \    |
    1   3   5        take A-C (1)
    |    \  |        take C-D (2)
    C --2-- D        reject A-D (3), A and D are already joined
                     take A-B (4)

                     MST = {A-C, C-D, A-B}, weight 7, 3 edges for 4 vertices
```

Work the example rather than trusting the picture. Note that the MST is not the set of the
three cheapest edges: A-D is cheaper than A-B and still gets thrown out, because B has to be
reached somehow and only the expensive edges reach it.

## The two algorithms

Both are greedy, and both are correct, which is unusual: greedy algorithms are normally wrong.

| | Kruskal | Prim |
|---|---|---|
| Grows | a forest that merges into one tree | one tree outward from a start vertex |
| Each step | take the globally cheapest edge that does not close a cycle | take the cheapest edge leaving the tree so far |
| Needs | edges sorted, plus a way to ask "already connected?" | a [[Heap]] of candidate edges |
| Cost | $O(E \log E)$ | $O(E \log V)$ |
| Better on | sparse graphs | dense graphs |

Kruskal's "already connected?" test is the interesting part: it is a union-find (disjoint-set)
structure, which answers the question in near-constant time and is the reason the sort
dominates the running time. The vault has no note on union-find; it belongs with
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]].

Prim's inner loop is almost exactly Dijkstra's. The only difference is what goes in the
priority queue: Prim stores the cost of the *edge* into the tree, Dijkstra the cost of the
whole *path* from the source. Two lines apart, two different problems.

## Why greedy works here

The **cut property**: split the vertices into any two groups, and the cheapest edge crossing
the split is in some MST. That is the whole justification, and both algorithms are it applied
differently. Prim cuts between "in the tree" and "not yet"; Kruskal's rejected edges are the
ones whose cut has already been crossed more cheaply.

The exchange argument that proves it is a [[Proof By Contradiction]]: assume an MST without
that cheapest crossing edge, add the edge (this makes exactly one cycle), and the cycle must
contain some other crossing edge, which is heavier. Swap them and the tree got cheaper, so the
original was not minimal.

If all edge weights are distinct the MST is unique; ties are what allow several.

## The company it keeps

MST is on the easy side of a line that runs right through graph problems. It is polynomial and
comfortable, along with shortest path and connectivity. Change the requirement slightly to
"visit every vertex in a cycle, cheapest" and you have the travelling salesman, the weighted
[[Hamiltonian Cycle]], which is [[NP-Complete]]. The MST is nonetheless useful there: it is a
lower bound on the tour, and doubling it gives an approximation.

Real uses: network and circuit layout, clustering (build the MST, delete the $k-1$ heaviest
edges, and the components are your clusters), and image segmentation.

## Core Facts to Know

- A spanning tree of $V$ vertices has exactly $V - 1$ edges and no cycles.
- The MST minimises total edge weight; it is unique when all weights are distinct.
- **Kruskal**: sort all edges, take the cheapest that does not close a cycle, using union-find.
- **Prim**: grow one tree, repeatedly taking the cheapest edge leaving it, using a [[Heap]].
- Both are greedy and both are provably optimal, via the **cut property**.
- Kruskal $O(E \log E)$, Prim $O(E \log V)$.
- Prim differs from Dijkstra only in what the priority queue holds.
- MST is polynomial; the travelling salesman version is [[NP-Complete]].
